outline.description: Introduce the problem of controlling large text-to-image diffusion models for downstream tasks. Motivate why careful finetuning is necessary, summarize the two target tasks (subject-driven generation and controllable generation), and list desiderata for finetuning (efficiency, stability, preservation of pretrained generative ability). Provide an overview of the Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT) idea and the chapter-by-chapter roadmap of the textbook.
sections: The rise of text-to-image diffusion models
Limits of prompt-only guidance and need for finetuning
Two downstream tasks: subject-driven and controllable generation
Desiderata for finetuning pretrained generative models
High-level idea of Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT)
Outline of the book and learning goals

outline.chapter_title: Background: Text-to-Image Diffusion Models and Popular Adaptation Methods
outline.description: Provide the necessary background about diffusion models used in text-to-image generation and common finetuning/adaptation techniques. Explain how existing methods approach subject-driven generation and controllable generation, and introduce baseline adaptation methods such as DreamBooth, LoRA, ControlNet and T2I-Adapter to set the stage for comparisons with OFT.
sections: Fundamentals of diffusion-based generative models
Latent vs pixel-space diffusion (Stable Diffusion, Imagen, GLIDE)
Model components: UNet, text encoders, attention layers
Subject-driven generation: DreamBooth and inversion-based approaches
Controllable generation: ControlNet, T2I-Adapter, image-to-image translation
Parameter-efficient finetuning methods: LoRA, adapters, low-rank updates
Common evaluation practices and datasets for text-to-image tasks

outline.description: Provide the mathematical tools and concepts used throughout the book: linear algebra basics, geometry of the hypersphere, cosine similarity and angular measures, orthogonal matrices and groups, and a primer on manifold-constrained optimization. This chapter equips readers with the formal language needed to understand OFT.
sections: Vectors, inner products and norms
Cosine similarity and angular distance
Unit hypersphere and geometry on S^{d-1}
Orthogonal matrices and special orthogonal group SO(d)
Skew-symmetric matrices and basic matrix identities
Manifold constrained optimization: Riemannian view brief
Spectral decomposition, phase/magnitude intuition from Fourier

outline.description: Introduce hyperspherical energy (HE) as a measure of pairwise neuron relations on the unit sphere, discuss its relevance to semantic encoding in neural networks, and present empirical and theoretical observations motivating HE preservation during finetuning. Include illustrative toy experiments (e.g., autoencoder phase/magnitude analogy) showing the importance of neuron directions.
sections: Definition of hyperspherical energy and motivations
Relation between HE and pairwise cosine similarities
Why neuron directions matter: empirical evidence and literature
Toy experiments: autoencoder study and phase/magnitude analogy
Interpretation of HE in pretrained networks
Why Euclidean distance is insufficient as a preservation metric
Implications of HE for finetuning design

outline.description: Present the core OFT idea: adapt a pretrained weight matrix via a layer-shared orthogonal transformation so that pairwise neuron angles (and thus hyperspherical energy) are preserved. Formulate the OFT objective, show equivalence to preserving hyperspherical energy, and discuss why orthogonal transformations are appropriate for finetuning semantic properties.
sections: Intuition: rotation/reflection preserves angles but can change semantics
Formal OFT forward pass for fully connected layers
Derivation: HE-preservation and orthogonality
Initialization and why start from identity
Interpretation: changing canonical coordinates vs changing neurons
Phase-spectrum analogy revisited: why angle changes effect semantics
Practical considerations for applying OFT to layers in networks

outline.description: Detail efficient ways to parameterize and optimize orthogonal matrices used in OFT. Cover Cayley transform and its properties, block-diagonal parametrization for parameter efficiency, block sharing, computational complexity analysis, and numerical stability considerations.
sections: Why naive orthogonalization is expensive (Gram–Schmidt, QR)
Cayley parameterization: formula, properties, and limitations
Special orthogonal group vs full orthogonal group (determinant 1 vs ±1)
Block-diagonal orthogonal matrices: motivation and design
Block sharing to further reduce parameter counts
Parameter count and complexity comparisons vs LoRA
Numerical stability, matrix inverse cost and practical tricks

outline.chapter_title: Constrained and Extended Variants: COFT and Re-scaled OFT
outline.description: Introduce two important variants: Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT), which enforces a radius/deviation constraint from identity for increased stability; and Re-scaled OFT, which adds per-neuron magnitude scaling. Explain mathematical formulations, enforcement strategies (e.g., projected gradient on skew-symmetric Q), and the trade-offs each variant provides.
sections: COFT formulation: orthogonality plus epsilon-deviation constraint
Neumann series approximation and mapping constraint to Q
Projected gradient descent for enforcing radius constraint
Re-scaled OFT: forward pass with diagonal scaling matrix
When to use COFT vs OFT vs Re-scaled OFT
Hyperparameters: epsilon, block size, learning rates
Empirical effects of constraints on stability and flexibility

outline.description: Compare OFT and its variants to established finetuning methods (LoRA, DreamBooth, ControlNet, T2I-Adapter). Analyze conceptual and mathematical differences: multiplicative orthogonal updates vs additive low-rank updates, parameter-efficiency trade-offs, and implications for stability and generalizability.
sections: Rewriting OFT as a multiplicative update and relation to additive updates
LoRA vs OFT: low-rank additive update vs block-orthogonal multiplicative update
Adapters and tuning mechanisms in Transformers
Why OFT can converge faster: manifold view and search space reduction
When additive updates may be preferable
No additional inference overhead: practical implications
Summary table of properties across finetuning methods

outline.description: Provide a practical recipe for implementing OFT in real models. Cover which layers to apply OFT to (attention, FFN, convolution), how to integrate into existing frameworks, optimization details, initialization, enforcing orthogonality in practice, memory and compute considerations, and debugging tips.
sections: Selecting layers for OFT in UNet / Transformer architectures
Applying OFT to attention weight matrices and convolutional kernels
Parameter initialization: identity R and zero Q
Optimization: learning rate schedules, regularization
Implementing Cayley transform and projected gradients efficiently
Memory and runtime profiling: block sizes and trade-offs
Common pitfalls, debugging, and reproducibility tips

outline.description: Explain experimental setups used to evaluate OFT: datasets, training paradigms for subject-driven and controllable generation, baseline selection, and the design of evaluation metrics including standard perceptual metrics and the newly proposed control consistency metric. Provide details needed to reproduce experiments.
sections: Datasets for subject-driven and controllable generation (COCO, ADE20K, CelebA-HQ)
Training regimens: DreamBooth-like pipeline and ControlNet-like pipeline
Baselines and fair-comparison principles
Perceptual and semantic metrics: CLIP-I, CLIP-T, DINO, LPIPS
Control consistency metric: motivation and computation per task
Protocol for convergence and stability experiments
Statistical considerations: seeds, sampling, and qualitative selection

outline.description: Present and analyze OFT's empirical findings on subject-driven generation. Cover convergence speed, finetuning stability, quantitative metrics, qualitative examples, human evaluation summaries, and ablation studies comparing OFT, COFT, DreamBooth, and LoRA.
sections: Experiment setup specific to DreamBooth comparisons
Convergence curves and stability analysis
Quantitative results: DINO, CLIP-I, CLIP-T, LPIPS
Qualitative examples and interpretations
Human evaluation methodology and outcomes
Ablations: effect of block size, COFT epsilon, number of finetuning steps
Failure cases and limitations observed

outline.description: Detail OFT's performance on controllable generation tasks (Canny-to-image, segmentation-to-image, landmark-to-face). Include convergence analysis, control consistency metric results, qualitative comparisons to ControlNet/T2I-Adapter/LoRA, data-efficiency findings, and more ablations.
sections: Task descriptions and dataset-specific settings (C2I, S2I, L2F)
Convergence speed comparisons and plots
Control consistency metrics: IoU/F1, mean IoU/accuracy, landmark L2
Qualitative comparisons: examples and failure modes
Data-efficiency experiments and results
Ablation studies: OFT vs COFT, block-sharing, rescaling
Interpretation of why OFT yields stronger controllability

outline.description: Synthesize theoretical and empirical insights explaining why OFT works. Discuss the manifold view of finetuning, trade-offs between flexibility and regularity, role of hyperspherical energy preservation, and connections to other theoretical results. Include proofs or derivations where appropriate (e.g., orthogonal invariance of pairwise cosine similarities and HE).
sections: Proof: orthogonal transforms preserve pairwise angles and hyperspherical energy
Manifold perspective: optimization on hypersphere vs Euclidean updates
Trade-off: flexibility (expressivity) vs regularity (stability)
Why small Euclidean deviation is insufficient to capture semantic preservation
The role of block structure as inductive bias
Connections to orthogonal over-parameterized training literature
Open theoretical questions and conjectures

outline.chapter_title: Limitations, Open Problems and Future Directions
outline.description: Critically evaluate OFT's limitations and outline open problems raised in the paper. Discuss scalability concerns with Cayley transform, parameter-efficiency bottlenecks, compositionality of orthogonal updates, and other promising research directions.
sections: Scalability challenges: matrix inverse, large d and block sizing
Bias introduced by block-diagonal parametrization and its consequences
Compositionality: multiplying orthogonal matrices for multi-tasking
Potential extensions: approximate orthogonal parametrizations, sparse/structured transforms
Combining OFT with other adaptation techniques (e.g., LoRA hybrids)
Better theoretical understanding of HE and downstream generalization
Research project ideas and next steps

Implement Cayley parameterization for small matrices
